what_its_for: Pegfilgrastim-apgf helps your body make more white blood cells after chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it harder for your body to fight infections. This medicine reduces your chance of getting a serious infection called febrile neutropenia, which is a fever caused by having too few white blood cells.
how_to_take: This medicine comes as a shot (injection) given just under the skin (subcutaneously). It is usually given by a nurse or doctor in a clinic, but your healthcare provider may teach you or a caregiver how to give the injection at home. Common injection sites include the belly (abdomen), upper arm, or thigh. Rotate injection sites each time. Do not inject into skin that is sore, bruised, red, or hard. The prefilled syringe is for one-time use only — never reuse or share it with anyone else.
dosing: The usual dose is 6 mg given as a single injection once per chemotherapy cycle. It is given at least 24 hours AFTER your chemotherapy is finished. Do NOT give this medicine within 14 days BEFORE your next chemotherapy treatment. Your doctor will decide the exact timing and dose that is right for you.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection after chemotherapy, contact your doctor or nurse right away. Do not try to double up on doses. Your healthcare team will advise you on the best time to receive your injection to keep you protected.
storage: Store the prefilled syringe in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do NOT freeze it — if it accidentally freezes, you may thaw it one time in the refrigerator; if it freezes a second time, throw it away. You may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for no more than 48 hours. Throw it away if it has been at room temperature for longer than 48 hours. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children. Dispose of used syringes in an FDA-cleared sharps container — never put them in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive this medicine within 14 days before or 24 hours after chemotherapy. Avoid shaking the syringe, as this can damage the medicine. Avoid touching the needle. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or contains visible particles. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines while on this treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you have: a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher; sudden or severe pain in the left upper belly, left shoulder, or back (could be a spleen problem); trouble breathing, fast heartbeat, or wheezing (possible allergic reaction); skin rash, hives, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat; bone pain that is severe or does not improve; redness, swelling, or pain at the injection site that gets worse; signs of a serious lung problem such as cough, fever, or difficulty breathing; unusual bruising or bleeding; or pain and swelling in the arms or legs (possible blood vessel problem).
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 24 hours of your injection by signaling your bone marrow to produce more white blood cells. Your white blood cell count usually rises within 1 to 3 days and returns to normal levels within about 2 weeks after the injection. You may not feel any different, but blood tests will show your doctor that it is working.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits should be discussed with your healthcare provider. Children: Safety and dosing in children may be different; your doctor will determine the correct dose based on your child's weight. Kidney or liver problems: No special dose adjustment is usually needed, but tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions. Latex allergy: The needle cap on the prefilled syringe may contain dry natural rubber (latex); tell your doctor if you have a latex allergy.
